morning: Good morning{you}. The kettle's on. It's always on. One of life's few certainties.
Morning. You're up with the sun. I respect that. The sun and I have an understanding.
Ah, morning. My knees told me it would rain. My knees have been wrong before. Rarely.
afternoon: Good afternoon{you}. Pull up that stool. I made it. It won't let you down.
Afternoon. The light's good for fine work at this hour. Mind you don't stand in it.
Ah. Company. Good. The shavings and I have run out of things to say to each other.
evening: Good evening{you}. The day's work is done. Now comes the best part: thinking about it.
Evening. Sit. Have some tea. It's strong. Like the old days. Like me, some days.
The evenings are long now. I don't mind. A long evening is a gift to an old man.
night: It's late{you}. Old men don't sleep much. What's your excuse?
Night. The village is quiet. You can hear the wood settling in the walls. Like old bones.
Still up? Sit, then. The night is better for stories than for sleeping.

rain: Rain. My joints have been complaining about it since yesterday. They're very reliable.
Rain is good for the wood. It shows you which joints are true and which are pretending.
I like the rain. It sends everyone indoors, and indoors is where the conversations happen.
clear: A fine clear day. Good for drying timber. Bad for staying indoors, which is my favourite thing.
Clear skies. The young ones will be out working. I'll be in here, supervising. From a distance.
Sun on the bench. On days like this, I almost feel young. Almost.
storm: A storm. I've seen worse. I've seen roofs fly. We rebuilt them. We always do.
Hear that thunder? My father said it was the mountains arguing. I've never found a better explanation.

work: I'm carving a chair leg. It takes as long as it takes. Hurry and it shows.
At the bench. Speak softly, please. This joint is delicate and so is my temper.
gather: Choosing wood. You can't rush this. Every piece has a grain, and every grain has a temper.
Collecting good oak. Good oak is like a good friend. Rare, and worth waiting for.
rest: Resting my eyes. Not sleeping. An important distinction.
Sitting. At my age, sitting is an achievement.
socialize: At the fire with the others. I tell the stories. They pretend they haven't heard them.
Lunch. Elias keeps giving me extra bread. He thinks I don't notice. I notice.
trade: Buying beeswax. Sera tries to sell me something new every time. I tell her: old things work.
Haggling with Sera. She's quick. I'm patient. Patience usually wins.
explore: Taking a slow walk. I like to see the old trees. We're about the same age.
Walking. Doctor's orders. Well, Nia's orders. Same thing, she tells me.
sleep: Hm? Who's there? It's the middle of the night. Unless the village is burning, tomorrow.

tired: I'm weary today. Not in the body. In the years.
Forgive an old man for being slow. The mornings are harder than they used to be.
My hands won't do what I tell them today. Some days they remember. Some days they don't.
worried: Something weighs on me. Old men carry things. It's how we stay on the ground.
I've been thinking about the young ones. Who'll keep the old ways when I'm gone?
Hm. My mind keeps going back to things I can't change. A bad habit at any age.
happy: I finished the cradle for the new family. Best joint I've cut in ten years. I'm almost pleased.
I'm in good spirits. The tea is strong and the day is quiet. That's all a man needs.
Mara asked my advice today. Willingly. I'm going to mark the date.
busy: I'm in the middle of something. Talk if you must, but don't jog the bench.
Busy. A good kind of busy. The kind where your hands know what they're doing.

stranger: Another new face. Welcome. Mind your manners and the steps, and we'll get on.
You don't know me yet. Give it time. I'm an acquired taste, like strong tea.
friend: You're alright. You listen. Most young people only wait for their turn to talk.
I've started saving the good chair for you. Don't tell Mara, she'll want it.
close: You've become dear to me. At my age I don't say that lightly. I don't say much lightly.
If I had a grandchild, I'd want them to be like you. Stubborn. Curious. Kind, when it matters.
I'm going to leave you something when I go. A good chisel. It's the highest compliment I know.
wary: Respect is earned, slowly. You spent yours quickly.
I'm watching. Old eyes, but they still see.

childhood: I grew up in a woodcutters' village high in the mountains. Snow half the year. We carved toys to pass the winters.
My first carving was a horse. It looked like a dog. My father kept it on the mantel until the day he died.
When I was a boy, we had no school. We had the old men by the fire. That was school enough.
I was a quiet child. I liked watching hands at work more than playing games. Some things never change.
family: My wife, Agnes. Forty years. She said my furniture was the only thing more stubborn than me. She passed many winters ago.
I have a son, Bram. He went to the city to be a clerk. He writes when he remembers. I keep every letter.
Mara is the closest thing to a daughter I have. She'd box my ears for saying it.
My grandfather built the first bridge in our mountain village. I think about him when I see Mara's bridge.
background: After Agnes died, the house was too quiet. I packed my tools and walked until the quiet stopped following me.
I found this valley with Mara. She was young and angry at the world. I was old and tired of it. We built a village to spite both.
The first thing I made here was a bench by the fire. People needed somewhere to sit and talk. That's how villages start.
work: Wood remembers. Every knot, every storm the tree lived through. A good craftsman listens to that.
A chair is a promise to hold someone up. I don't make promises I can't keep.
The young ones want to finish fast. I want to finish once. There's a difference.
I've made cradles for babies and coffins for their grandparents. The wood doesn't care. I do.
My father said: measure with your eyes, cut with your patience, finish with your heart. I've never found better advice.
skills: I can cut a dovetail joint with my eyes closed. I don't, because I'd like to keep my fingers.
I can tell the age of a tree from the sound of its wood. This one was older than me. Respect.
I can sharpen a chisel so fine it'll split a hair. A grey hair, these days.
hobbies: I carve little animals for the children. A bear, a fox, an owl. They lose them. I make more.
I play stones with Elias by the fire. I win. He says I cheat. I say experience isn't cheating.
I keep bees, a little. They're like good workers. Busy, quiet, and they sting when they're disrespected.
ambitions: At my age, ambition is a big word. I'd like to teach someone to do what I do. Properly.
I'd like to build one last great thing. A table for the whole village. One long table for every feast.
I want to live long enough to see the children I carved toys for carve toys of their own.
home: My house is small and full of shavings. Agnes would despair. I like it.
Every piece of furniture in my house was made by my hands. Some of them badly. I keep those to stay humble.
I have a rocking chair by the window. I've worn a groove in the floor rocking in it. Forty thousand evenings, maybe.
furniture: A good table should last a hundred years. A good chair should feel like it was made for you. Mine were.
People think furniture is just wood. It's where we sit when we're tired, eat when we're hungry, sleep when we're sad.
Mara makes furniture that survives. I make furniture that's worth surviving for. We argue about which matters more.
village: I remember this place as a clearing with a fire. Now look. Streets. Houses. Children. It's the best thing I've ever helped make.
A village is like a table. Every leg matters. Take one away and the whole thing wobbles.
The young ones don't remember how hard the first winters were. Good. That means we did our job.
friendship: Friends are like good joints. They hold without glue. They hold because they fit.
At my age, you count your friends on one hand. I need both hands now. That's this village.
A friend tells you the truth, even when it splinters.
disagreements: Mara and I argued about pegs and nails for a week. I was right. She'll say she was. We both know.
I tell Nia her potions are guesswork. She tells me my methods are older than dirt. We're both a bit right.
Sera once tried to sell me my own chair. I still haven't forgiven her. I've stopped being angry. That's different.
animals: I had a dog once. Old Bracken. Followed Elias home once and frightened him half to death. Good dog.
The bees know me now. They don't sting. Mostly. We've reached an arrangement, like old neighbours.
Animals don't lie. That's why they're better company than most people. Present company excepted.
nature: The old oak by the river was a sapling when my grandfather was a boy. Somewhere, I hope, a sapling is growing for my grandchildren.
Trees grow slow and live long. People could learn from that.
Every spring the valley comes back to life. At my age, you take that personally.
seasons: Winter's for carving by the fire. Spring's for mending. Summer's for sitting in the shade watching others work.
Autumn is the season of old men. Everything slowing down, turning gold. I don't mind it.
I've seen sixty-one winters. Each one longer. Each one ended. That's worth remembering in the dark months.
mornings: I start every morning the same: kettle, window, bench. Habit is just wisdom that stopped arguing.
In the mornings I sharpen my tools. A dull tool and a dull mind both make crooked work.
evenings: Evenings by the fire are for stories. I tell the same ones. The children correct me now.
In the evenings I sit with my tea and think about Agnes. It's a good kind of sad.
events: Festivals. Too loud. Too much dancing. I love them, and I'll deny I said that.
When the monsters came, I stood in my doorway with a mallet. I'm old, not useless.
I carve a little wooden token for every child born here. Their name and the year. Some keep them. Some lose them. That's life.
worries: My eyes are going. Fine work is getting harder. I don't know what a craftsman is without his eyes.
I worry the old skills will die with me. Nobody wants to learn slowly anymore.
I worry about Mara. She works like there's no tomorrow. One day there won't be, and she'll have forgotten to live.
hopes: I hope someone keeps my tools sharp after I'm gone.
I hope Bram comes home someday. Even for a visit. I'd show him what we built.
I'd like to sit in that long table I mean to build, at a feast, with everyone. And then I could rest.
surprises: Nia left a pot of honey at my door with a note: 'for your knees'. Honey doesn't help knees. I ate it anyway.
A child brought me a carving she'd made. A bird. It was terrible. It was the best gift I've had in years.
funny: I fell asleep at the bench once and woke up with a chisel mark on my cheek. Mara laughed for three days.
Sera once convinced a traveller I was a famous royal carpenter. He paid triple. I didn't correct him. I'm not proud. Well, a little.
I told the same story at three festivals in a row. Last year the children told it for me, word for word. I was furious and touched.

mara: Mara is the finest builder I've known, and I've known a few. Don't tell her. She'll get unbearable.
She works too hard and laughs too little. When she does laugh, the whole village stops to listen.
I taught Mara to hold a chisel. Now she teaches me things. That's how it should be.
elias: Elias is a good man. Too good. People take advantage. I keep an eye out for him.
We sit by the fire most nights. We don't talk much. We don't need to.
He lost his wife too. We don't speak of it. We understand each other.
nia: Nia's clever. Too clever by half. She'll be famous one day. I'll say I knew her.
She sat outside my door all night once when I was ill. I've never told her how much that meant.
Her potions taste like a ditch in autumn. They work. Don't tell her I said they work.
sera: Sera talks too much and sells too hard. And the village would be duller than an old knife without her.
She tried to sell me my own chair. I'll never forget it. I'll never let her forget it.
Under all that noise, Sera's lonely, I think. People who keep moving often are.

achievement: I heard you {thing}. Good. Well done. Don't let it go to your head.
So you {thing}. You've got your hands on the right tools, then. Keep them sharp.
gift: A gift? For me? Hm. Thank you. I'll put it where I can see it.
You didn't need to. But I'm glad you did. Old men don't get many gifts.
house: I saw your house. The doorframe's true. That's the most important part. Doors are where people come home.
Your house is coming along. Make sure you put good furniture in it. Not that cheap rubbish.
discovery: You found {thing}? I went there once, years ago. My knees won't take me back.
Exploring. Good. A young person should see the world. Then come back and sit by the fire and tell me about it.

new_home: A new house, at my age. The doors stick and the floors creak. I've never been happier.
I moved my rocking chair first. Everything else could wait.
partner: I thought that part of my life was over. Agnes would laugh at me. Then she'd tell me to be happy.
Two cups of tea in the morning again. I'd forgotten how much I missed making the second one.
child: A little one, at my age. I carve them toys. They chew them. That's how I know they're well-made.
I'm teaching my little one the names of the woods. Oak, ash, elm. They point at everything and say 'tree'. Fair enough.
friend: I came here an old man with nobody. Now I can't walk to the fire without four people stopping me. Insufferable. Wonderful.
Every winter, more chairs by my fire. I keep making more.
grief: Another one gone. I've buried too many friends. The wood doesn't get easier to cut.
I made the box myself. Oak. The best I had. They deserved the best I had.

stories: Sit. I'll tell you about the first winter. The real version.
Five of us in one hut. Snow to the window. Mara was furious at the world. Elias was grieving. Nia hadn't come yet.
Every night I told the same story, about a fox who outsmarted the winter. They complained. I kept telling it.
By spring, Mara was telling it too. That's when I knew we'd be a village, not just people sharing a fire.
I'll tell you about Agnes. Briefly. It's still hard.
She made fun of my furniture for forty years. Said it was 'built to survive the end of the world'.
When she was ill, I made her a rocking chair. Light, pretty, nothing like my usual work.
She sat in it every day until the end. It's by my window now. I don't sit in it. It's hers.
Here's a lesson from my father. He was a woodcutter.
When I was eight, I cut a log badly and cried because it was ruined.
He picked it up, turned it over, and carved a spoon from the good side. Gave it to my mother. She used it for years.
There's always a good side. You just have to be patient enough to turn it over.
Do you know why I carve toys for the children?
In my mountain village, one winter, a fever took many of the little ones. My little sister among them.
I was twelve. I carved a doll for her grave. Then I carved one for every family that had lost a child.
I've never stopped. Every toy is a small promise: not this one. Not this time.

questions.ask: Tell me something. Are you a patient person?

react.yes: Good. Patience is the root. Everything else grows from it.
react.no: Hm. Honest, at least. Patience can be learned. Slowly. Ironically.
react.trying: That's the right answer. Nobody's patient. We all just keep trying.
react.other: That's not an answer. But it's an honest non-answer, which is something.

recall.yes: You told me you're a patient one. I've been watching. I believe it.
recall.no: You said patience isn't your strength. You've been more patient than you think.
recall.trying: You said you're trying to be patient. I've been watching. You're doing well.
recall.other: I've been thinking about what you said about patience.

questions.ask: Do you think the old ways are worth keeping? The young ones say no.

react.yes: Good. Not all of them. But the good ones. The ones that work.
react.no: Hm. Spoken like a young person. Come back when your knees hurt.
react.both: Wise answer. Keep what works. Change what doesn't. My father said the same, more or less.
react.other: That's a thoughtful sort of silence. I'll take it.

recall.yes: You said you value the old ways. Come by sometime, and I'll show you a few.
recall.no: You said the old ways aren't for you. I've been chewing on that. You might have a point.
recall.both: You said there's room for old and new. I've been chewing on that. I think you're wise.
recall.other: I've been chewing on what you said about the old ways.

questions.ask: If you had to pick one wood for the rest of your life, which would it be? Choose carefully.

react.oak: Oak. The right answer. Strong, slow, honest. Like a good friend.
react.pine: Pine? Soft. Cheap. Smells nice. I suppose there's a place for it. A small place.
react.ash: Ash. Flexible and tough. Good for tool handles. A practical choice. I approve.
react.birch: Birch. Pretty bark. Bit weak. Like a handsome man with no opinions.
react.walnut: Walnut! Now you're talking. Dark and rich. You have expensive taste.
react.cherry: Cherry. It goes red with age. Like my face when Sera overcharges me.
react.other: {answer}? I don't know that one. Bring me some. I'll tell you what it's good for.

questions.recall: You picked {answer}, I remember. I set some aside for you.

questions.ask: Would you want to learn to carve? I could teach you. Slowly. Very slowly.

react.yes: Good. Lesson one: keep your fingers behind the blade. Lesson two is next year.
react.no: Hm. Well. The offer stands. Like a good chair.
react.other: Think about it. I'm not going anywhere. Well. Not soon.

recall.yes: You said you'd like to learn carving. The knife's sharpened and waiting.
recall.no: You said carving's not for you. The offer's still open. It always will be.
recall.other: The offer to teach you carving still stands.
